W1.title: Research planner
W1.instruction: Plans where to look. For every company: founders’ and key personnel’s LinkedIn posts and interviews, press, job posts. For a publicly listed company, also: public transcripts (earnings calls, investor calls), investor presentations, annual reports. For a warm approach, also the notes, emails and transcripts of the earlier contact in the Case File
W1.guard: Names the people to cover (founders, CEO, CFO, CTO, function heads)

W1.title: Research agent
W1.instruction: Collects passages where the company or its leaders describe problems, priorities, spend, failures and targets
W1.guard: Each record keeps URL, date, speaker and exact passage

W1.title: Evidence verifier
W1.instruction: Re-opens every source and confirms the passage exists, is attributed correctly and is within the recency window
W1.guard: Unverifiable evidence is dropped, never paraphrased into a claim

W1.title: Pain point extractor
W1.instruction: Turns evidence into candidate pain points in the company’s own terms
W1.guard: No candidate without at least one verified evidence record

W1.title: Pain point ranker
W1.instruction: Scores every candidate on the rubric below and picks the five biggest; fit to Mindmap only breaks ties
W1.output: Top 5, with scores per factor and reasons
W1.guard: The count of five and the weights are configuration values (Section 18)

W1.title: Specificity checker (fresh context)
W1.instruction: Tests all five on the same bar: stated by this company? would it read the same for any company in the industry? how strong is the evidence?
W1.output: Pass or fail per item, with an explanation of why it is a real problem the company itself has listed, citing the evidence
W1.guard: A passing example: the founder says AI spend is running heavy and the models are not optimised, which an orchestrator agent can address. A failing example: a fifth item such as invoice processing with no evidence or explanation. A failed item is replaced from the pool; if the pool runs out, the consultant decides whether to show fewer than five (added; see A.2)

W1.title: Consultant gate
W1.instruction: Approves the five pain points and their sources
W1.guard: Nothing downstream starts before this gate

W1.title: Periodic table builder
W1.instruction: Builds the periodic table of the many use cases that can be employed at this company. Candidate tiles come from the accelerator catalogue in the knowledge base, filtered to the functions and processes the research shows this company runs; the tile count fills the periodic table template’s grid (read from the template, not fixed). Tiles are grouped by function. If fewer applicable tiles remain than the grid holds, the grid is filled from applicable catalogue items for adjacent functions, never with generic tiles; if none remain, the consultant decides at W1-G2
W1.guard: A fresh-context check removes any tile that does not apply to this company’s business (for example a function it does not have) and any generic AI item; each tile carries a one-line description written for this company

W1.title: Solution designer
W1.instruction: For each pain point: the solution, how it works in three to five steps, the accelerator it uses, the value it brings. Then stars and numbers the five priority tiles on the periodic table to match slide 3, adding and starring a tile for any priority solution that is a new build with no catalogue accelerator
W1.output: Five solution specs; priority tiles starred
W1.guard: Each spec opens by restating its pain point and source; new builds are flagged where no accelerator fits

W1.title: Solution architect agent
W1.instruction: Draws one solution architecture per solution in the Mindmap format
W1.guard: In the solution architecture format (Appendix B.1); component names identical to the solution spec; every data source named, web sources included: the system or file the W1 research shows the company runs or, where the research does not show it, the most likely one, proposed and flagged for W1-G2; never a generic tile (HR-17, B.1)

W1.title: Demo shortlister
W1.instruction: Uses the W2 matching logic to pick one to three demos or videos for the next-steps slide

W1.title: Deck assembler
W1.instruction: Builds each slide by duplicating its template slide from the template library and editing it (7.2, Appendix B.3). Never creates a new slide. If a slide type has no template in the library, the deck holds here and the consultant is asked for the template
W1.guard: Text and images change; font sizes and formatting untouched (HR-12)

W1.title: S2 QC, W1 profile
W1.instruction: Runs the W1 checks (13.3) until two consecutive clean loops

W1.title: Follow-on
W1.instruction: Proposes a W8 email as a follow-on (5.5): cold outreach for a cold approach, follow-up for a warm one
W1.guard: The email is drafted only once the consultant accepts the follow-on; it then runs through W8 with its own QC and gate

W2.title: Library matcher
W2.instruction: Searches the demo and video library by industry, function, process and the client’s pain points
W2.guard: Library entries are tagged by industry, process, sub-agents and the client each was built for

W2.title: Fit reviewer
W2.instruction: Checks each candidate against the client: does it show the topic or problem they raised? would anything in it confuse or contradict the W1 story?
W2.output: One to three picks, or none
W2.guard: Below the match threshold nothing is shown and W6 is proposed (added; see A.2)

W2.title: Talk track writer
W2.instruction: Per pick: which problem it answers, which screens to show, what result to point to

W2.title: Branding and data check
W2.instruction: Confirms the build platform is not visible and no other client’s data appears in the chosen demo or video

W2.title: S2 QC, W2 profile
W2.instruction: D8 on every claim in the talk track; D4 for free demo or POC offers and price or timeline promises

W2.title: Consultant gate
W2.instruction: Approves the picks and the talk track

W3.title: Recording intake (Transcription service)
W3.instruction: Pulls the recording, and tl;dv’s own transcript where one exists, by tl;dv meeting link, or takes an upload. W3-1 to W3-3 run once, at intake (RT2), for every workflow that receives a recording; they are listed here because W3 depends on them most
W3.guard: No step-specific rule

W3.title: Media converter (Transcription service)
W3.instruction: Converts the video to MP3
W3.guard: Done as a separate step today; the agent automates it

W3.title: Transcriber (Transcription service)
W3.instruction: Converts the MP3 to a transcript with speaker labels and timestamps
W3.guard: Also a separate step today. When tl;dv supplies a usable transcript, W3-2 and W3-3 are both skipped (added; see A.2)

W3.title: Transcript preparer
W3.instruction: Maps speakers to attendees and their titles; segments by topic (added; see A.2)
W3.guard: Titles feed the complexity parameter

W3.title: Requirement extractor
W3.instruction: Pulls requirements, pain points, user roles, current process cues, volumes, FTEs, KPIs (for example DSO), constraints, budget and timeline signals, decision makers
W3.guard: Nothing extracted without a timestamp

W3.title: Consolidator
W3.instruction: Merges all calls, emails and documents; later statements supersede earlier ones and conflicts are flagged (added; see A.2)
W3.guard: Both statements kept and cited where they conflict

W3.title: Understanding reviewers (2 by default, 3 if the consultant sets it; fresh context)
W3.instruction: Each rebuilds the requirement summary from the sources alone by a different method (6.3): one call by call; one as the client’s decision maker deciding what they are buying; when a third runs, one for delivery feasibility, read as the team that must build it. Each then compares its summary with the register
W3.guard: Differences go to the consultant

W3.title: Consultant gate
W3.instruction: Confirms the requirement summary and re-confirms the parameters
W3.guard: No step-specific rule

W3.title: Solution designer
W3.instruction: Designs the solution per requirement, reusing accelerators
W3.guard: Every element maps to a baseline requirement; nothing unrequested

W3.title: Architects
W3.instruction: High-level solution architecture and technical architecture in the Mindmap formats
W3.guard: Formats in Appendix B.1 and B.2. Depth set by complexity. Team standing preferences: where no source tech stack exists, the real production technology is specified; each named technology is explained; each use case is its own standalone flow (data origin, steps, technology); every data source in both architectures is named, the system or file and the data taken from it, never a generic tile (HR-17, B.1)

W3.title: Architect gate
W3.instruction: Approves the technical design
W3.guard: No step-specific rule

W3.title: Provisional phase plan (delivery lead, with agent support)
W3.instruction: Phases, durations, dependencies and milestones for the Gantt, from the approved design and comparable past projects
W3.guard: Not man hours. Man hours are estimated in the commercials step (W3-19), in the order the brief gives; the deep QC (W3-20) reconciles the two

W3.title: Process flow builder
W3.instruction: As-is and to-be flows per process in the B.4 format: one swimlane per sub-process; as-is cards tagged with the user role or system that does the step; to-be cards tagged with the platform component, as in the reference deck, and with the user role that acts on or receives the step’s output, so each user’s value is visible; a process summary per process; a solution heat map when the solution spans several areas (B.4)
W3.guard: Format in Appendix B.4. As-is is usually estimated, by the method in 9.4

W3.title: Plan and governance builder
W3.instruction: Gantt chart for the timeline from the provisional phase plan; RACI matrix in the governance section
W3.guard: Roles match the delivery team; durations are reconciled with the reviewed man hours at W3-20

W3.title: ROI builder
W3.instruction: Waterfall from today’s cost to the future state, one bar per lever. Baseline bars come from client-stated FTE counts, costs and KPIs (for example DSO), each cited; FTEs become cost only with a client-stated or consultant-confirmed cost per FTE. Each lever’s improvement is estimated from the approved solution design and comparable past deployments in the knowledge base, recorded internally with its basis, and shown to the client as approximate
W3.guard: Only if FTE or KPI baselines exist; every number cites its source or its recorded basis; shows the client’s own cost levers only, never Mindmap’s price, fees or a payback on them (HR-05)

W3.title: Drafting agent
W3.instruction: Writes the proposal in the variant structure (9.2) and the audience profile (5.4): a detailed document in the Mindmap proposal template (until that template is uploaded, B.5, a detailed document holds at this step and the consultant is asked for it; the agent never invents a layout), or a PPT proposal by duplicating and editing the provided template slides
W3.guard: Never creates a slide (HR-12); a slide type with no template holds the draft and the consultant is asked for one; the Word template for detailed documents is pending (B.5)

W3.title: Visual planner and cohesion pass
W3.instruction: Incorporates the diagrams from W3-9 to W3-13; scans every section for further diagram opportunities and adds them (9.3) without dropping any content; then checks one style and one set of component and role names across every diagram and the text
W3.guard: No step-specific rule

W3.title: QC before the first draft
W3.instruction: D1 twice; D2, then D3 twice, where any contradiction triggers the escalation protocol (13.4); then D4, D5 and D8, whose findings are fixed without escalation
W3.output: First draft after two consecutive clean loops
W3.guard: No step-specific rule

W3.title: QC on the first draft
W3.instruction: D1 2 to 3 passes (a third pass runs whenever pass 2 raises a finding); D2, then D3 twice, with any contradiction revised and the loop re-run; D4 and D5
W3.guard: Mirrors W4 Stage E (added; see A.2)

W3.title: D6 proofread
W3.instruction: Every word, by AI; minor findings fixed
W3.guard: No step-specific rule

W3.title: Human proofread
W3.instruction: The consultant reads every word. A critical or major issue, or any issue QC did not log, triggers the escalation protocol and the work returns to W3-17
W3.guard: No step-specific rule

W3.title: S1: effort, cost, price, commercials table
W3.instruction: Man hours estimated and checked by the QC-1 and QC-2 agents (12.1, S1-G1); then cost, indicative infrastructure cost, revenue share where it applies, recommended price and its approval (12.2, S1-G2); then the one commercials table (12.4)
W3.guard: No step-specific rule

W3.title: Deep QC
W3.instruction: D7, D3 and D6 on the whole document, checking the commercials section and every change since W3-G3 first: all commercial terms in place; prices only in the one commercials table, none in the executive summary or anywhere else; numbers consistent everywhere; the Gantt reconciled with the reviewed man hours (a mismatch updates the Gantt); the approved price checked against the format bands, with a band change sent to the consultant before release
W3.guard: Revise and re-run until clean

W3.title: Release gate
W3.instruction: The consultant reads the commercials section and every change since W3-G3, then releases. A critical or major issue, or any issue QC did not log: escalation protocol (13.4), back to W3-20, or to W3-17 if it lies outside the commercials
W3.guard: A W8 cover email is proposed as a follow-on (5.5)

W4.title: RFP parser
W4.instruction: Splits the RFP and annexures into clauses, including tables, forms and scoring grids
W4.guard: Clause count reconciled against the RFP’s own numbering; gaps shown

W4.title: Source collector
W4.instruction: Gathers call transcripts with updates (recordings go through the Transcription service, 6.4), the buyer’s answers to the questions we asked (RFI answers), corrigenda and addenda

W4.title: Consolidation agent
W4.instruction: Consolidates the three together into one structured requirement register
W4.guard: Where a later source changes a clause, both are kept, the prevailing one marked, both cited

W4.title: Core requirement analyst
W4.instruction: Separates the core benefit the RFP is buying from supporting features, mandatory compliance and evaluation weights; writes the core preliminary requirement
W4.guard: An RFP for a platform that does X, with AI features on top, is a platform bid: the focus is the core platform; the AI features are answered but not emphasised

W4.title: Unbiased reviewers (3 by default; 2 if the bid owner sets it at RT7)
W4.instruction: Each starts from blank, takes all the information into consideration, writes its own detailed understanding first, then compares it with the preliminary statement
W4.output: Independent understanding and gap list each
W4.guard: Different methods (clause by clause; the evaluator’s scoring view; the requirements as read by the delivery team that must build them, the method dropped when only two run) so the same input does not produce the same answer; no access to Agent 1’s reasoning; each returns a coverage log of every clause, transcript and RFI answer it read (6.3 item 3)

W4.title: Reconciler
W4.instruction: Sets the reviews side by side: agreements, disagreements, misreads, emphasis errors
W4.guard: No averaging; every disagreement goes to the bid owner

W4.title: Bid owner gate
W4.instruction: Resolves disagreements and locks the requirement baseline
W4.guard: Every later check measures against it

W4.title: Response planner
W4.instruction: Outline in the buyer’s order, compliance matrix skeleton, page budget weighted to the core requirement and the scoring
W4.guard: Buyer section order, page limits and forms followed exactly

W4.title: Solution designer and architects
W4.instruction: Solution, high-level solution architecture, technical architecture
W4.guard: Same guards as W3-9: Mindmap formats, real production technology where no source stack exists, each technology explained, each use case its own standalone flow; every element maps to a baseline requirement; every data source named, as in W3-9 (HR-17, B.1)

W4.title: Architect gate
W4.instruction: Approves the technical design

W4.title: Provisional phase plan (delivery lead, with agent support)
W4.instruction: Phases, durations, dependencies and milestones for the Gantt
W4.guard: Not man hours. Man hours come in the commercials step (W4-22), in the order the brief gives; the deep QC (W4-23) reconciles the two

W4.title: Drafting agent
W4.instruction: Builds the preliminary proposal in the buyer’s format; where none is prescribed, in the format the bands select (5.4): the Mindmap detailed document template (pending, B.5; until it is uploaded, a detailed document holds here and the bid owner is asked for it, and the agent never invents a layout), or a PPT built by duplicating and editing the provided template slides. Fills the compliance matrix (added; see A.2)
W4.guard: Full compliance is the default and the target: every requirement is answered as complies wherever it can be met; where one cannot be met, the drafting agent records a proposed partial compliance or deviation with its reason; the bid owner decides it as soon as it is raised (a decision on that requirement, which does not hold the stage), and only approved ones appear, each stated once; never creates a slide (HR-12)

W4.title: Visual engine
W4.instruction: Incorporates all diagrams: architectures, as-is and to-be flows (as-is estimated by the method in 9.4), Gantt from the provisional phase plan, RACI, ROI waterfall if data exists; then adds a diagram wherever a section’s content calls for one (9.3)
W4.guard: Same rules as W3-11 to W3-13 and W3-15: as-is and to-be tagging (B.4); Gantt and RACI reconciled with the reviewed man hours at W4-23; ROI only from cited baselines, shown as approximate; same component and role names as the text; every data source named (HR-17); no content dropped

W4.title: Check 1: D1 compliance, pass 1
W4.instruction: Checks every line, word, image and table for compliance with the requirements, against the RFP, transcripts, RFI answers and the baseline

W4.title: Check 2: D1 compliance, pass 2
W4.instruction: The same compliance check by a new instance, briefed to make sure nothing is missed

W4.title: Check 3: D2 contradiction agent
W4.instruction: Takes the requirement understanding and reads the document for any sort of contradiction, flagging each one

W4.title: Checks 4 and 5: D3 internal contradiction and consistency, run two times
W4.instruction: Contradiction within the document itself and consistency, for example SMS used for a flow, then “secure because we do not use SMS”; each run by a new instance

W4.title: D4, D5 and D8
W4.instruction: Unrequested scope such as a mobile app; diagrams and tables against the text; sources of claims about the client. These findings are fixed without escalation; the loop re-runs until two consecutive clean loops (13.2, 13.5)

W4.title: First draft
W4.instruction: Reached after two consecutive clean loops of W4-12 to W4-16

W4.title: D1 compliance, 2 to 3 passes (a third pass runs whenever pass 2 raises a finding)
W4.instruction: New instances check that everything complies with the requirements

W4.title: D2, then D3 twice
W4.instruction: Looks for contradictions again; any found is revised and the stage restarts at W4-18

W4.title: D4 and D5
W4.instruction: Findings fixed without escalation; the stage repeats until two consecutive clean loops

W4.title: D6 proofread
W4.instruction: Every word, by AI; minor findings fixed

W4.title: Human proofread
W4.instruction: The bid owner proofreads every word. A critical or major issue, or any issue QC did not log, is a QC escape: the escalation protocol runs and the work returns to W4-18

W4.title: S1: effort, cost, price, commercials table
W4.instruction: Man hours estimated and checked by the QC-1 and QC-2 agents (12.1, S1-G1); then cost, indicative infrastructure cost, revenue share where it applies, recommended price and its approval (12.2, S1-G2); then the one commercials table (12.4). Where the buyer mandates a price schedule, it is filled instead

W4.title: Deep QC
W4.instruction: D7, D3 and D6 on the whole document, checking the commercials section and every change since W4-G3 first: all commercial terms in place, prices only in the commercials table and nowhere else (including the executive summary), numbers consistent across the document, the Gantt reconciled with the reviewed man hours; where the buyer set no format, the approved price checked against the format bands, with a band change sent to the bid owner; revise and re-run until clean

W4.title: Submission check
W4.instruction: Buyer submission instructions: forms, declarations, signatures, file naming, page limits, number of copies (added; see A.2). Any change it makes goes back through the deep QC (W4-23) for the changed parts before sign-off

W4.title: Bid owner sign-off
W4.instruction: Reads the commercials section and every change since W4-G3, then releases. A critical or major issue, or any issue QC did not log: escalation protocol (13.4), back to W4-23, or to W4-18 if it lies outside the commercials. A W8 submission note is proposed as a follow-on (5.5)

W5.title: Context study
W5.instruction: Studies the details of every document, transcript and earlier answer the client has sent; builds a provisional requirement register, using the W4 Stage A agents (W4-1 to W4-4) for an RFP, or the W3 extractor and consolidator (W3-5, W3-6) otherwise; recordings go through the Transcription service (6.4)
W5.guard: No question is written before this completes

W5.title: Question drafter
W5.instruction: Drafts candidate questions from the documents
W5.guard: Each tied to a clause or passage; no target to produce many

W5.title: Agent 1: already-answered check
W5.instruction: For each question, searches all sources for the answer. Found: the question is dropped, citing where. Not found: the sections searched are recorded
W5.output: Kept and dropped lists with evidence

W5.title: Agent 2: relevance check
W5.instruction: Keeps a question only if it is really needed: its answer changes design, effort, price, compliance or risk; states which

W5.title: Agent 3: solution simulation
W5.instruction: Simulates building the proposal (architecture, effort, plan, commercials) and records where it gets stuck; those stuck points become questions, and questions that unblock nothing are dropped (added; see A.2)
W5.guard: Questions added here also pass W5-3 and W5-4

W5.title: Section verifier
W5.instruction: Re-opens the section each question cites and confirms the problem is really there, as described

W5.title: Simplifier
W5.instruction: Writes each question in simple English beside the complex version
W5.guard: The complex column keeps the document reference so people can trace where each question comes from

W5.title: Duplicate and contradiction check
W5.instruction: Merges questions asking the same thing; removes questions that contradict each other or the provisional register
W5.guard: The same question is never asked twice

W5.title: Ranker
W5.instruction: Ranks by impact and trims to the configured cap (added; see A.2); questions cut by the cap are listed for the approver at W5-G1

W5.title: S2 QC, W5 profile
W5.instruction: W5-3, W5-4, W5-6 and W5-8 repeated 2 to 3 times by new instances; D6 proofread; the anonymised Q&A rule (HR-11) and the build platform rule (HR-03)

W5.title: Manual cross-check assist
W5.instruction: For each question, shows side by side: the question, the section it cites with the passage quoted, the closest answering passage found anywhere in the sources, and the sections searched. It is briefed to prove the question unnecessary, not to confirm it
W5.guard: Pass rule: a question reaches W5-G1 only with either its cited passage quoted word for word and located, or, for a gap found by the W5-5 simulation, the stuck point described and the list of sections searched showing the information is absent; a question with neither is dropped. Fallback: if, over the first pursuits, the approver still finds already-answered or irrelevant questions above the configured rate, the consultant or bid owner switches the cross-check at W5-G1 to human-led, with the agent supplying search hits only; each escape is added to the W5-3 and W5-4 checklists (ESC-4). The pass rule is tested on two past RFPs with their RFI question sets and final responses (pending, B.5)

W5.title: Approver gate (bid owner for an RFP; presales consultant otherwise)
W5.instruction: Manually reviews every question: already answered? relevant? is the problem really in the cited section?

W6.title: Domain capture, with research support
W6.instruction: The domain owner, the team member who studied the domain, records how the work really flows: sequence, decision points, branches. A research agent supports with sources and fills gaps, each flagged for review
W6.guard: The team’s understanding is the primary input, because Claude alone gives a generic process that will not impress a client

W6.title: Domain owner gate
W6.instruction: Approves the process map before anything is built

W6.title: Business problem selector
W6.instruction: Picks the real business problems in that domain that the demo must solve
W6.guard: Tied to the client’s pain points where known

W6.title: Process decomposer
W6.instruction: Breaks the process into 10 to 12 sub-agents and specifies each to the depth it deserves (14.2)
W6.guard: The count range comes from config. Each spec covers its sub-flows and branching, not a single step

W6.title: Impact feature designer
W6.instruction: Proposes features that impress this audience because they are rarely seen in applications, such as a 3D view; a feature counts only if this audience does not already see it in its own tools (the brief’s exception: drawing applications already show 3D)

W6.title: UI designer
W6.instruction: Designs an interface that looks very good and passes the UI checklist (14.3)

W6.title: Builder
W6.instruction: Builds every sub-agent as functional, inside the platform
W6.guard: Nothing hardcoded; values come from uploaded documents and configuration (HR-13)

W6.title: Test data preparer
W6.instruction: Assembles in-sample and out-of-sample documents, with expected outputs for each sub-agent
W6.guard: Document parsing gets the widest test set

W6.title: Test agent
W6.instruction: Runs every sub-agent end to end through the browser (Playwright and Claude in Chrome) and compares outputs with expected; document parsing is tested on every document type
W6.guard: Empty, wrong or generic outputs fail; a failed sub-agent returns to W6-6 with its test log. Automated testing only serves to a certain extent

W6.title: S2 QC, W6 profile
W6.instruction: D1 (spec against build, including a check for hardcoded values), D4 (no build platform name, no unagreed claims), D5 (UI checklist)

W6.title: Output review
W6.instruction: The domain owner, consultant and demo builder review the outputs themselves, confirm they are what they expect, and check the demo against the acceptance criteria in 14.3
W6.guard: Automated tests never replace this review

W6.title: Run sheet writer
W6.instruction: The demo path, the data to load, talking points tied to the pain points
W6.guard: Used for a live demo or by W7

W7.title: Script writer
W7.instruction: Writes a run sheet first if W6-10 has none; then the script, scene by scene: the client problem, what the sub-agent does, the result
W7.guard: Each scene tied to a pain point

W7.title: Recorder
W7.instruction: Records the scripted path, driven by browser automation so takes repeat

W7.title: Voiceover
W7.instruction: AI voiceover from the script; voice, accent and pace set per client region

W7.title: Editor
W7.instruction: Cuts, zooms on key outputs, captions, Mindmap title and end cards

W7.title: Build platform frame check
W7.instruction: Checks every frame: the platform name in the URL bar, at the bottom of the page (where it sometimes appears), in the tab title, on loading screens
W7.output: Pass, or frames to crop or mask

W7.title: S2 QC, W7 profile
W7.instruction: D3 (script against screens), D4, D5 (frames), D6 (captions)

W7.title: Consultant gate
W7.instruction: The consultant and the demo builder watch the final cut
W7.output: Release; the video is sent with a W8 cover note as a follow-on (5.5), or the demo is shown live from the W6-10 run sheet

W8.title: Context reader
W8.instruction: Pulls only the facts the email may use from the Case File

W8.title: Drafter
W8.instruction: Writes the email, short by default
W8.output: Calm, measured, consultant tone; no hype (HR-10)
W8.guard: Calm, measured, consultant tone; no hype (HR-10)

W8.title: S2 QC, W8 profile
W8.instruction: D8 on every claim; D4 removes any free demo, free POC, price or timeline commitment; D6 proofreads every word and the tone; every pattern in the table below is checked

W8.title: Consultant gate
W8.instruction: Proofreads every word, edits and sends
W8.output: Sending is always a human action
W8.guard: Sending is always a human action

S1.title: Work breakdown agent
S1.instruction: Breaks the approved solution into work packages: each module and sub-agent, integrations, data work, testing, deployment, project management
S1.guard: Every package maps to a baseline requirement

S1.title: Estimator
S1.instruction: Estimates the man hours needed per package and role

S1.title: QC-1 agent (fresh context)
S1.instruction: Reviews the estimate package by package: missing packages, wrong roles, hours too high or too low, weak assumptions

S1.title: QC-2 agent (fresh context)
S1.instruction: Reviews the corrected estimate independently to make sure the man hours are correct

S1.title: Reconciler
S1.instruction: Applies agreed changes; differences above the configured tolerance go to the solution architect and the delivery lead with reasons; compares the total effort with the provisional phase plan and flags any gap for the Gantt

S1.title: Cost calculator
S1.instruction: Human cost = reviewed man hours × blended hourly rate. Then estimates the reduction from using AI in development, per work package: which tasks AI speeds up (for example code generation, test writing, documentation, data mapping), by how much, and why, checked by a fresh-context reviewer. Then overhead
S1.guard: All values from config; nothing hardcoded. The overhead within the 20% to 30% range is proposed by the delivery lead from the engagement’s load (travel and onsite time, project management and governance, compliance and documentation, number of client stakeholders), with the reason recorded. The overhead and the AI reduction are approved at S1-G2; reduction ranges per task type come from config

S1.title: Infrastructure estimator
S1.instruction: Estimates the indicative infrastructure cost from the approved technical architecture: hosting option (cloud, client data centre or on-premise), compute and GPU, storage, model or API usage at the expected volumes, third-party licences
S1.output: Indicative infrastructure cost with its assumptions
S1.guard: Given most of the time; charged to the client at actuals with no Mindmap margin; the assumptions stay internal and a one-line basis appears in the table; a licence or paid data feed billed directly by its provider is shown on its own row instead (12.4)

S1.title: Revenue share modeller
S1.instruction: Platform or SaaS builds only: proposes a revenue share from the models in config (for example a percentage of platform revenue, a fee per transaction, or a fee per active user), with the basis, the rate, the term, and any floor, cap or reduced implementation fee it trades against
S1.guard: Not run for a standard build

S1.title: Price recommender
S1.instruction: Recommends the client price from the internal cost, client size, deal size, budget signals from calls and comparable past deals, with its reasoning on what the client is likely to pay and move ahead with

S1.title: Pricing owner
S1.instruction: Approves or sets the client price, the AI reduction, the overhead, whether the infrastructure line shows the indicative amount from S1-7 or reads “At actuals” (reason recorded) and, for platform builds, the revenue share (added; see A.2)

S1.title: Commercials table builder
S1.instruction: Builds the single client commercials table (12.4)
S1.guard: The calling workflow then runs the deep QC (W3-20, W4-23)

house_rules.Rule: Never offer a free demo or a free POC
No deliverable outside the baseline or agreed scope (for example a mobile app, extra integrations, SLAs)
The build platform (Base44), its functions and integrations are never named or visible in client content

No internal cost basis in client outputs: man hours, hourly rates, overhead, AI reduction, margin, notes on where the team is stretched. Where a buyer-mandated price schedule (W4) requires effort or rates, the pricing owner decides at S1-G2 what is shown, and D7 checks against that decision

house_rules.Rule: Prices only in the one commercials table; never in the executive summary or anywhere else. In W4, where the buyer mandates a price schedule, that schedule replaces the commercials table and this rule applies wherever its format allows (12.4)

The infrastructure line always appears, highlighted and bold, stating that it is charged as actuals and billed directly to the client, not by Mindmap. Most of the time it carries an indicative amount; where none is given (the pricing owner decides at S1-G2, with the reason recorded), the amount reads “At actuals”. In W4, where the buyer mandates a price schedule, the infrastructure line follows that schedule wherever its format allows (12.4)
No POC content or POC timings in use case slides
